rationale: A wins because it keeps the story shapes sharp without spending facts it does not have. A's "Companies are paying an average of $342,000 a year for software nobody is using" is a clean data angle; B's "The first AI agents in finance departments aren't doing the math" is a clever line that walks into an unsupported claim. B has strong proof lists, but too many headlines overdraw the account.
gaps_in_A: "whose revenue model is threatened" runs hotter than the supplied facts. The update shows buyer-side audit pressure, not proven vendor revenue damage.
"AI agents are moving into real finance work" is the softest headline in A; it could become generic agentic-AI fog unless the approval-flow and rejection-rate proof exists.
"monetization deferred to a future enterprise tier" is plausible, but still an inference. The update says an enterprise tier is coming, not exactly how Ramp will monetize it.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp's new agent cancels your software subscriptions" overstates the product. The update says it drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails that finance approves.
"SaaS pricing has depended on customers not auditing their own seat counts closely" is a sweeping market claim with no support in the update.
"The first AI agents in finance departments aren't doing the math" is unsupported and partly contradicted by the facts: the agent scans spend and flags duplicate or unused seats.
"charging for the approval workflow" turns an announced enterprise tier with custom approval workflows into a pricing claim the update does not give.
